title: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
summary: Find bugs before attackers do: coverage-guided fuzzing with libFuzzer and AFL++, sanitizers, harnesses, crash triage, symbolic execution, variant analysis, AI-assisted discovery and coordinated disclosure.
outcomes: Explain how AFL's edge bitmap and corpus evolution let a fuzzer reach code random inputs cannot
Write fast, deterministic libFuzzer, Go and Atheris harnesses, including structure-aware ones
Choose the sanitizer that detects a given bug class and read its report to find the root cause
Deduplicate and minimise crashes, then turn the reproducer into a fix and a regression test
Judge fuzzer comparisons using trials, run length, seeds and ground truth (Klees et al. 2018)
Use an SMT solver and variant analysis to reach hard paths and find sibling bugs
Write a reproducible vulnerability report and follow coordinated disclosure timelines

lessons.title: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under

blocks.md:
A **bug** is any place where a program does something its authors did not intend. A **vulnerability** is a bug that lets someone break a security property: read data they should not see, change data they should not change, or stop a service. **Vulnerability research** is the craft of finding vulnerabilities on purpose, proving they are real, explaining their cause and getting them fixed.

A tiny example. A parser copies a name field into a 16-byte buffer and trusts a length byte from the input. With a length of 3 nothing goes wrong. With a length of 23 the copy writes 7 bytes past the buffer. The memory-safety-bugs course showed what such a heap overflow can lead to; this course is about how to *find* it before anyone else does, and what to do next.

This course follows one path and stops deliberately:

1. **Find**: make the program misbehave, usually with a fuzzer (a tool that feeds it huge numbers of generated inputs).
2. **Triage**: decide whether the crash is new, real and security relevant.
3. **Root-cause**: find the exact line and the wrong assumption.
4. **Report**: write it up so the maintainers can reproduce it.
5. **Fix**: a patch plus a regression test, so the bug never returns.

Turning a crash into a working attack (*weaponising* it) is a different job. It is not taught here, and a good report almost never needs it: a sanitizer report and a reproducer are proof enough for any serious maintainer.

blocks.title: From crash to fix: the path this course teaches

scenes.caption: Research starts with finding behaviour the authors did not intend: a crash, a sanitizer report, a wrong answer.
Most crashes are duplicates or harmless. Triage sorts them and shrinks each input to the smallest one that still fails.
Root-causing finds the line and the broken assumption, for example 'the length byte is never larger than the buffer'.
The report goes privately to the people who can fix it. They patch and add a regression test; an advisory follows.
The dashed branch is exploit development. This course deliberately stops before it: crash, triage, root cause, report, fix.

blocks.md:
**Authorisation comes first.** The security-basics course named the laws: the US CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act) and the UK Computer Misuse Act make unauthorised access a crime whatever your intent. In practice:

- Fuzzing **your own code**, or open-source code you build and run on your own machine, needs nobody's permission.
- Testing **someone else's running system** (a website, an API, a device you do not own) needs written permission, for example a bug bounty programme's published scope.
- A **safe harbour** clause is a promise in such a programme not to pursue legal action against research done within its scope and rules. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) disclosure cheat sheet warns that stepping outside the scope may be a criminal offence, and that some countries restrict reverse engineering even of software you installed yourself.

**Coordinated disclosure** is the norm this course follows: report privately, give the maintainers time to fix, then publish so users learn they must update. Two other models exist. *Private disclosure* tells only the vendor and leaves publication to them; *full disclosure* publishes everything at once, usually as a last resort against a vendor that ignores reports. The OWASP cheat sheet adds rules that keep you on the right side of the line: never demand payment as a condition of reporting (that can be extortion), redact any personal data from evidence, and check whether your employment contract lets you report bugs found at work.

Fuzzing a live service you do not own is not 'just sending inputs'. Millions of malformed requests are an attack from the operator's point of view, can take the service down, and are unauthorised access under the laws above. Fuzz local builds; test hosted systems only inside a written scope.
Vulnerability research is a loop of find, triage, root-cause, report, fix. Its output is a fixed bug and a regression test, not an exploit, and it starts with permission.

blocks.question: You find a crash by fuzzing a library on your laptop, then notice a company runs the same library on its public API. What is the right next step?
options: Report the bug to the library's maintainers privately, with your local reproducer
Send the crashing input to the company's API to confirm it is affected
Publish the reproducer immediately so users can protect themselves
Ask the company for a reward before telling them anything
blocks.explain: Your local reproduction is already proof. Hitting the company's API is testing a system you have no permission to test, publishing first leaves every user exposed, and demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. The maintainers can fix it for everyone, including that company.

blocks.question: Which statement best separates a bug from a vulnerability?
options: Vulnerabilities are always memory corruption; bugs are logic errors
Bugs crash, vulnerabilities never crash
A vulnerability is a bug that lets someone break a security property such as confidentiality or integrity
A bug becomes a vulnerability once it has a CVE number
blocks.explain: Security impact is the difference. Many vulnerabilities are logic flaws, many crash, and the CVE identifier is just a label assigned after the fact.

lessons.title: Fuzzing from a stormy night in 1988: random, mutation, generation

blocks.md:
In the autumn of 1988 Barton Miller, a computer science professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, was logged in to a Unix machine over a 1200 baud dial-up modem during a thunderstorm. Line noise corrupted what Miller typed, and to Miller's surprise the noise made common Unix utilities crash. That semester Miller added a project to the graduate Advanced Operating Systems course (CS736): build a program that outputs a random character stream, feed it to as many utilities as possible, and work out which inputs break them.

Miller needed a name for this kind of testing and wanted one that would "evoke the feeling of random, unstructured data", and settled on **fuzz**. Of three student groups, Lars Fredriksen and Bryan So succeeded: the 1990 paper reports that they could crash or hang between 25 and 33 percent of the utilities on the seven Unix variants they tested.

Miller's classic fuzzing has three traits, per the project's page: the input is random, there is no model of the program (*black box*, the program is an opaque box), and the test oracle is simple: a crash or hang is a failure. An **oracle** is whatever decides whether a run passed. The team repeated the study in 1995, 2000 (Windows NT), 2006 (macOS) and 2020, and published the tools, raw results and suggested fixes each time.

Random bytes have a weakness you can measure. Below is a Miller-style fuzzer against a small Python decoder that only accepts input starting with the five bytes `TLV1N`.

blocks.code:
import os, random
import tlvlib                  # decode(): checks b"TLV1N", then reads a length byte

random.seed(1988)
passed_magic = crashes = 0
for _ in range(1_000_000):
    data = os.urandom(random.randint(0, 16))     # pure random bytes, Miller style
    if data[:5] == b"TLV1N":
        passed_magic += 1
    try:
        tlvlib.decode(data)
    except ValueError:
        pass                                     # expected rejection
    except Exception:
        crashes += 1                             # anything else is a bug
print("inputs: 1000000  passed magic:", passed_magic, " crashes:", crashes)

# real output on the course machine (1.7 s):
# inputs: 1000000  passed magic: 0  crashes: 0
blocks.caption: A million random inputs never got past the 5-byte magic check, so the bug behind it (shown in the Python lesson) stayed hidden. The chance per input is 1 in 2 to the power 40.
At a million inputs per second that is about 13 days of nonstop fuzzing for this one 5-byte check, and every further exact byte multiplies the wait by 256.

blocks.md:
Three families of fuzzers grew from this:

- **Random** (Miller's original): fresh random data each time. Cheap, but stuck at the first check that needs specific bytes.
- **Mutation-based**: start from valid sample inputs (*seeds*) and change them a little: flip bits, change bytes, insert, delete, splice two inputs together. The result is usually *almost* valid, so it passes early checks and reaches deeper code.
- **Generation-based**: build inputs from a model of the format or protocol (a grammar or a state machine). Codenomicon, a Finnish security testing company, sold **Defensics**, a model-based protocol testing suite in this family; its engineers found Heartbleed in 2014 while improving Defensics' SafeGuard feature.

Modern fuzzers add **feedback**: they watch which code each input reaches and keep the inputs that reach new code. That is the next lesson.

blocks.title: Three ways to make the next test input

scenes.caption: A valid seed: magic TLV1, record type N, a length byte (hex 03) and the 3-byte name 'bob'.
Random: every byte is fresh noise. The magic check fails on the first byte almost every time.
Mutation: copy the seed and change one byte, here the length 03 becomes 17 (23 in decimal). Magic still passes, so the length handling gets tested.
Generation: build a new input from a model of the format. Every record is well formed, but values (type, length, content) are chosen to probe edge cases.

blocks.md: Miller's own summary of fuzzing, written in a foreword years later: it is not meant to replace systematic testing, it is one more tool, "albeit an extremely easy one to use". Run it early and often.

blocks.question: A format starts with a 4-byte magic number and a CRC (checksum) over the whole file. Which fuzzer family is most likely to get past both checks with no extra help?
options: Pure random bytes
Generation from a model that computes the CRC for every input
Mutation of valid seeds, with no knowledge of the CRC
All three are equally likely
blocks.explain: Mutation keeps the magic but almost every mutation breaks the CRC, so the parser rejects it early. A generator that knows the format recomputes the checksum, so its inputs reach the code behind it. (libFuzzer's docs suggest a third route: a fuzzing build that skips checksum verification.)

blocks.question: What did Miller's original fuzz study use as its oracle?
options: A specification of each utility's correct output
Code coverage reached by each input
A comparison with a second implementation
Whether the program crashed or hung
blocks.explain: The oracle was deliberately simple: crash or hang means fail. That is why it could be automated across many programs and operating systems with no model of what each program should do.

lessons.title: Coverage-guided fuzzing: how AFL's edge bitmap steers mutation

blocks.md:
Michał Zalewski, a security researcher at Google (known online as lcamtuf), wrote **AFL** (American Fuzzy Lop; Zalewski's earlier fuzzer was called bunny-the-fuzzer). AFL made one idea practical: a fuzzer should *keep* any mutated input that makes the program do something new, and build on it. Over thousands of generations the kept inputs evolve into a collection that exercises far more of the program than random or plain mutation can.

To know whether an input did "something new", AFL needs **coverage**: a record of which parts of the code ran. The compiler inserts a few instructions at every branch point (*instrumentation*). The program then runs at nearly normal speed and leaves behind a map of what it did.

After each run the fuzzer compares the map with a global map of everything seen so far:

- A new edge means a new **tuple** (AFL's word for a source and destination pair): keep the input in the queue.
- A changed hit count also counts, but only when it crosses a **bucket** boundary: 1, 2, 3, 4-7, 8-15, 16-31, 32-127, 128+. A loop going from 47 to 48 iterations is ignored; a block running twice instead of once is not.
- Otherwise the input is thrown away.

The figure runs four traces of a toy program through a 16-slot map, using real XOR arithmetic with block numbers A=4, B=11, C=3, D=6, E=12.

blocks.title: AFL's edge bitmap, simplified to 16 slots

scenes.caption: Trace 1, A B C D E. The edges (entry,A) (A,B) (B,C) (C,D) (D,E) land in slots 4, 9, 6, 7, 15. All are new, so the input joins the queue.
Trace 2, A B D C E: the same five blocks in another order. Edges (B,D) (D,C) (C,E) give slots 3, 0, 13, never seen before. Kept.
Trace 3, A B C A E: a jump back from C to A (slot 5) and then A to E (slot 14). Two new tuples, so this input is kept too.
Trace 4 loops A B C three times then ends C D E. Every edge was seen before, but slots 6 and 9 hit 3 times and slot 5 twice: new buckets, so AFL keeps it.
A mutation that repeats trace 1 exactly sets only seen slots with seen counts. Nothing new: discarded. This keep or discard rule is the whole evolutionary engine.

blocks.md:
Why 64 kB? The whitepaper says most targets have 2,000 to 10,000 discoverable branches, where collisions (two edges sharing a slot) stay rare: about 1.5 percent of tuples at 2,000 branches and 7 percent at 10,000. The map is also small enough to compare in microseconds and to sit in the CPU's L2 cache.

The kept inputs form the **queue** (also called the **corpus**). AFL picks entries from it, mutates them, and adds whatever is new. Entries supplement but never replace earlier finds, so the fuzzer can explore different features of a format in parallel. For most targets, the whitepaper says, the queue grows to 1,000 to 10,000 entries.

blocks.title: Edges reached on GNU patch with different guidance (AFL whitepaper)

scenes.caption: Zalewski's experiment: GNU patch 2.7.3 seeded with a dummy text file, one pass over the queue. The seed alone reaches 163 edges.
Blind fuzzing (mutation without feedback), looped for a comparable number of runs, reaches 265 edges.
Keeping inputs that reach new blocks gets 1,130 edges; new edges, 2,070; AFL's full model with hit-count buckets, 2,597. Feedback is worth roughly ten times more code reached here.

blocks.md:
AFL also popularised **trimming** (removing parts of a kept input that do not change its path, since small files are faster and mutations land on the parts that matter) and a set of mostly deterministic early mutations: walking bit flips, adding and subtracting small integers, inserting "interesting" values such as 0, 1 and INT_MAX, before random stacked changes and splicing.

AFL itself has not been updated since 2017. Its community successor [AFL++](https://aflplus.plus/) ("the daughter of the American Fuzzy Lop fuzzer", in its maintainers' words) merges years of research improvements, adds binary-only modes through QEMU (Quick Emulator, an open-source machine emulator) and other emulators, and is what you install today. The next lesson uses **libFuzzer**, the same idea built into the LLVM compiler project.

blocks.prompt: A mutated input takes exactly the same edges as an input already in the queue, but one loop runs 50 times instead of 40. Will AFL keep it?
blocks.reveal: No. 40 and 50 both fall in the 32-127 bucket, so the hit-count signal does not change and the input is discarded. If the loop ran 30 times (16-31 bucket) it would be kept. Buckets make AFL sensitive to qualitative changes (once vs twice) and blind to small quantitative ones, which keeps the queue from filling with near copies.

blocks.question: Why does AFL record edges (pairs of blocks) rather than just which blocks ran?
options: Edges use less memory than blocks
Two inputs can visit the same blocks in a different order, and the order often matters for bugs
Blocks cannot be instrumented by a compiler
Edges make the program run faster
blocks.explain: The whitepaper's example: A B C D E and A B D C E reach identical blocks but different edges. Security bugs often come from unexpected state transitions, which only edge coverage sees.

blocks.question: What does the shift in prev_location = cur_location >> 1 achieve?
options: It makes A then B land in a different slot from B then A, and keeps a block jumping to itself distinct
It halves the map size
It randomises block numbers at run time
It counts how many times each block ran
blocks.explain: Without the shift, A XOR B equals B XOR A, and A XOR A is zero for every block, so direction and tight loops would be lost. Shifting the previous location breaks that symmetry.

lessons.title: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash

blocks.md:
**libFuzzer** is, in its documentation's words, "an in-process, coverage-guided, evolutionary fuzzing engine". *In-process* means it is a library linked into the program under test, calling your code in a loop with no new process per input, which is why it runs hundreds of thousands of inputs per second. Coverage comes from LLVM's SanitizerCoverage instrumentation, the compiler-inserted counters of the last lesson. (Its original authors have since moved on to a newer engine called Centipede; libFuzzer still gets bug fixes and is used everywhere.)

The target for this lesson is a small parser for an invented format, TLV (type, length, value: each record is a type byte, a length byte, then that many bytes). It has one planted bug, the one from lesson 1.

blocks.caption: tlv.c. The length check on line 14 only proves the value fits in the input, not in the 16-byte name field.

blocks.md: You connect libFuzzer to code with a **harness** (or *fuzz target*): a function named `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` that receives the fuzzer's bytes and passes them to the code under test. Building with `-fsanitize=fuzzer,address` links libFuzzer's `main` and turns on AddressSanitizer (ASan), which the memory-safety-bugs course introduced: it turns silent memory corruption into an immediate report.

blocks.caption: The harness allocates a fresh struct on the heap each run, so ASan can see writes past its 20 bytes. It returns 0 for every input; rejecting bad input is the parser's job, not a crash.

blocks.md: Started with an empty corpus directory, the real run on the course machine (Apple M-series, Homebrew clang 22) found the bug in about half a second. Each status line is an event: `NEW` means an input reached new coverage and joined the corpus, `REDUCE` means a smaller input with the same features replaced one. The libFuzzer docs define the fields: `cov` is edges or blocks covered, `ft` is *features* (coverage plus hit-count signals), `corp` is corpus entries and bytes, `lim` is the current input length limit, and `MS` lists the mutations that produced the input.

blocks.caption: Real output, trimmed ("..." marks removed fields and lines). Wall time for the whole run: 0.52 s. The crash file holds the 114-byte input that triggered the report.

blocks.md:
Look at execution #1045: `MS: ... CMP- DE: "TLV1"`. Random mutation did not guess the magic. libFuzzer builds with `-fsanitize-coverage=trace-cmp` by default, which reports the operands of comparisons (and of `memcmp`) back to the fuzzer. It saw the program compare input bytes against `TLV1` and put that string into the input as a dictionary entry (`DE`). This is how modern fuzzers get past the check that defeated a million random inputs in lesson 2.

The animation shows a simplified lineage of how a crashing input grows, using the mutation operators that appear in the log.

blocks.title: From empty input to crash: a simplified mutation lineage

scenes.caption: Execution #12: a few random bytes. The magic check fails at the first byte; only the rejection path is covered.
CMP mutation: libFuzzer saw memcmp compare input with 'TLV1' and copied those bytes in. New coverage (the loop), so the input is kept.
InsertByte adds a record: type 'N' with length 3 and value 'bob'. The N branch is new coverage. Kept.
ChangeByte turns the length into 17 hex (23) and InsertRepeatedBytes adds enough value bytes for line 14's check to pass.
memcpy writes 23 bytes into a 16-byte field of a 20-byte object. ASan stops the program and the fuzzer saves the input as crash-...

blocks.md: On macOS, Apple's Xcode clang ships without libFuzzer (the Atheris documentation says the same), and Homebrew's clang needs the SDK path (`-isysroot $(xcrun --show-sdk-path)`) to find system headers. On Linux, distribution clang packages include it.

A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

blocks.question: In the run log, what does the line '#1045 NEW cov: 6 ... DE: "TLV1"' tell you?
options: The fuzzer crashed at execution 1045
The user supplied a dictionary file containing TLV1
Input number 1045 reached new coverage, built with a dictionary entry TLV1 that comparison tracing discovered
The corpus was minimised to 6 inputs
blocks.explain: NEW means new coverage and a new corpus entry; the DE field names the dictionary entry used. No dictionary file was supplied: trace-cmp observed the comparison against TLV1 and learned the token.

blocks.question: Why does the harness allocate the struct with calloc inside LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput instead of using one global struct?
options: calloc is faster than a global
libFuzzer forbids global variables
Globals cannot be written by memcpy
A fresh object per run keeps runs independent and lets ASan put redzones around exactly 20 bytes
blocks.explain: State left over from a previous input makes results irreproducible, and a heap object gets ASan redzones right after its last byte. (A global would also get redzones, but leftover state between runs is the bigger problem.)

lessons.title: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware

blocks.md:
Real code often fights these rules. A random number generator seeded from the clock makes two identical inputs take different paths; a checksum on every chunk (PNG has a CRC per chunk) rejects nearly every mutation. libFuzzer proposes one build macro for all such cases, `FUZZING_BUILD_MODE_UNSAFE_FOR_PRODUCTION`, under which the project seeds its generator with a constant or skips checksum verification. The name is the warning: such a build must never ship.

A second problem is **structure**. Many APIs do not take one byte buffer: they take a mode flag, an integer, two strings. **FuzzedDataProvider** (FDP), a single-header C++ library shipped with LLVM, splits the fuzzer's bytes into typed values with calls like `ConsumeIntegral`, `ConsumeBool`, `ConsumeRandomLengthString` and `PickValueInArray`, so the harness can build well-formed calls or files from raw bytes.

blocks.caption: A structure-aware harness for the same parser. It always writes the magic and correct record framing, so every input exercises record handling. Compiled with clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address and linked with tlv.c.

blocks.md:
Three real runs of the TLV parser, each with seed 1, compare what gets the fuzzer past the magic check:

1. Raw-bytes harness with comparison tracing turned **off** (`-use_cmp=0 -use_memmem=0`) and no dictionary: 36,464,292 runs in 31 seconds, coverage stuck at 4, no crash.
2. The same, plus a two-line **dictionary** file (`magic="TLV1"` and `name="N"`): crash shortly after execution 6,413.
3. Default settings (comparison tracing on): crash shortly after execution 33,022, as in the last lesson.

And the FDP harness above, with comparison tracing off: crash shortly after execution 6,383, with a stack overflow this time, because `rec r` lives on the stack.

blocks.title: Coverage reached on the raw TLV harness (real runs, seed 1)

scenes.caption: With no way to learn the magic, 36 million inputs in 31 s cover 4 edges: the rejection path. No crash.
A dictionary hands the fuzzer the token TLV1. It reaches the record loop and the N branch (11 edges) and crashes within about 6,500 runs.
Default comparison tracing learns the token by itself and also reaches 11 edges and the crash, after about 33,000 runs. Either way, the bug is behind one check.

blocks.md: The best-documented lesson about harness reach comes from Google's Big Sleep team, an AI vulnerability research project (covered in lesson 15), and OSS-Fuzz, Google's free continuous fuzzing service for open source (lesson 10). In 2024 their AI agent found a stack buffer underflow in SQLite's `generate_series` extension, a bug so new it had not yet reached an official release. Their explanation for why fuzzing missed it: the OSS-Fuzz harness was not built with the `generate_series` extension enabled, and SQLite's alternative fuzzingshell.c harness carried an older, unaffected copy of the function. Then they tried fuzzing the right binary with AFL, with the needed keywords already in the corpus, and the bug was still not found after 150 CPU-hours. Coverage-guided fuzzing is strong on the code you point it at and blind to the code you do not.

Check what your harness reaches. libFuzzer and OSS-Fuzz can produce coverage reports; read them and look for important functions with zero hits. A missing build flag or an unregistered extension can hide a whole subsystem.

A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

blocks.question: Your harness calls a function that writes a log line and appends to a global cache on every call. What two problems does this cause?
options: Logging slows every run, and the global cache makes later runs depend on earlier inputs, so crashes may not reproduce
None, as long as the program does not crash
libFuzzer refuses to compile code with globals
The global cache is counted as new coverage, which is good
blocks.explain: The libFuzzer docs ask for fast targets without logging and without global state. A cache carried between runs means a crash can depend on a sequence of inputs, and the saved single input will not reproduce it.

blocks.question: Why did the FuzzedDataProvider harness find the bug quickly even with comparison tracing off?
options: FDP disables AddressSanitizer
FDP contains a list of known bugs
It writes the magic and the record framing itself, so every input is structurally valid and only values are fuzzed
It runs more inputs per second than a raw harness
blocks.explain: Structure-aware harnesses move the format's rigid parts into code. The fuzzer's bytes only choose types, lengths and contents, so no effort is wasted on inputs the parser rejects at the first check.

lessons.title: Sanitizers as oracles: which bug each one catches

blocks.md:
A fuzzer finds bugs only if something notices them. Without help, the oracle is "did it crash?", and many memory bugs do not crash. A **sanitizer** is a compiler option that adds run-time checks for one family of bugs. The memory-safety-bugs course introduced AddressSanitizer; here are the four you will use, named for what each one watches:

- **ASan** (AddressSanitizer): out-of-bounds reads and writes on heap, stack and globals, use-after-free, double free; leaks through its LeakSanitizer part. Typical slowdown 2x.
- **UBSan** (UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer): undefined behaviour in C and C++, such as signed integer overflow, out-of-range shifts, misaligned or null pointer use, and out-of-bounds array subscripts whose bounds are known at compile time.
- **MSan** ([MemorySanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/MemorySanitizer.html)): reads of uninitialised memory. Typical slowdown 3x. Linux, NetBSD and FreeBSD only.
- **TSan** ([ThreadSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSanitizer.html)): data races between threads. Typical slowdown 5x to 15x, memory 5x to 10x.

blocks.title: Which sanitizer reports which bug (1 yes, 0.5 partly, 0 no)

scenes.caption: ASan covers the classic memory-corruption family: out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, double free and (through LeakSanitizer) leaks.
UBSan catches arithmetic and pointer misuse. Its bounds checks only work where the compiler knows the array size, so overflows get a half.
MSan is the only one that sees a read of memory nobody wrote. TSan is the only one that sees two threads racing. Each needs its own build.
Read across a row before a campaign: whichever bug class you fear, make sure some build in your fuzzing setup has the sanitizer that sees it.

blocks.md: Two real runs on the course Mac show what UBSan and TSan reports look like. The first program computes a buffer size as `count * 4096` in a signed `int`; the second has two threads incrementing an unprotected global counter 100,000 times each.
