blocks.md:
Sanitizers have limits you must know, or you will trust a silent run too much:

- **They see only what runs.** A bug in code the fuzzer never reaches is never reported.
- **They cannot all be combined.** ASan, MSan and TSan each need their own *shadow memory* (a parallel map describing every byte of program memory). On the course machine `clang -fsanitize=address,thread` fails with "invalid argument '-fsanitize=address' not allowed with '-fsanitize=thread'", and `-fsanitize=memory` is "unsupported" on macOS. Large projects run separate fuzzing builds per sanitizer.
- **Granularity.** ASan guards the edges of each *allocation*, not each field. In the TLV parser, a 20-byte name write overflows `name[16]` into `count`, but stays inside the 20-byte struct.

blocks.title: What ASan can and cannot see in struct rec

scenes.caption: The 20-byte object: name[16] (shown compressed) then count[4]. ASan marks the bytes after the allocation as a redzone (rz).
A 16-byte name write fills exactly the field. Correct, silent.
A 20-byte write overwrites count too. Real run: no report, because every byte is inside the allocation. The program just has a corrupted count.
A 23-byte write reaches the redzone. ASan reports heap-buffer-overflow, '0 bytes after 20-byte region'. Intra-object overflows need assertions or a smarter oracle.

blocks.md: Assertions are oracles too. An `assert(len <= sizeof out->name)` would have caught the 20-byte case. Big Sleep's SQLite bug was caught by a debug assertion that release builds compile out: fuzz with assertions enabled.

blocks.question: A fuzzing campaign on a multithreaded image decoder has run under ASan for a week with no reports. Which bug class is it most likely still missing entirely?
options: Heap buffer overflows
Data races and reads of uninitialised memory
Use-after-free
Stack buffer overflows
blocks.explain: ASan covers out-of-bounds and use-after-free. Races need a TSan build and uninitialised reads need an MSan build (on Linux), and neither can be combined with ASan.

blocks.question: The TSan run printed hits = 200000, the correct total. Why is the report still a real bug?
options: It is not; the output proves the code is correct
TSan always reports false positives on counters
The total is only correct because of TSan
A race is undefined behaviour; this run got lucky, other compilers, optimisation levels or timings can lose updates
blocks.explain: TSan reports the unsynchronised access itself, not a wrong answer. Correct output on one run proves nothing about the next one, which is exactly why a race detector beats checking results.

blocks.md:
Three inputs shape every fuzzing campaign before the first mutation:

- **Seeds**: the starting corpus. A handful of small, valid, varied files (one per feature of the format) lets mutation start deep in the parser instead of rediscovering the format from nothing. Taking seeds from a project's own test suite is the usual first step.
- **Dictionaries**: tokens the format uses (keywords, magic numbers, tag names). The fuzzer splices them into inputs. libFuzzer and AFL share a syntax: one entry per line, `name="value"`, with `\xAB` for raw bytes.
- **Corpus maintenance**: as the corpus grows, many entries become redundant. Minimising it keeps fuzzing fast and makes it a useful regression suite.

AFL's whitepaper explains why dictionaries punch above their weight: when tokens are combined randomly, coverage feedback separates the meaningless combinations from the ones that trigger new behaviour, so the fuzzer "incrementally builds" grammar on top of them. With dictionaries it reconstructed the grammar of verbose formats such as JavaScript, SQL and XML. AFL can also build an *auto dictionary* by noticing runs of bytes where any flip changes the path the same way, a sign of a comparison against a constant.

The last lesson measured this on the TLV parser: with comparison tracing off, a two-line dictionary was the difference between 36 million fruitless runs and a crash in about 6,500.

blocks.code:
# tlv.dict  (libFuzzer / AFL dictionary format)
magic="TLV1"
name="N"
count="C"
maxlen="\xff"

# use it
./fuzz_tlv -dict=tlv.dict corpus/

# corpus minimisation: copy into MIN only the inputs that add coverage
mkdir MIN && ./fuzz_tlv -merge=1 MIN corpus/
#   MERGE-OUTER: 33 new files with 44 new features added; 12 new coverage edges

# AFL++ equivalents: afl-fuzz -x tlv.dict ... ; afl-cmin -i corpus -o MIN -- ./target @@
blocks.caption: The merge line is the real output for a 33-file corpus from a 20-second run of the fixed parser. On a parser this small every file carried a unique feature, so all 33 were kept; on real projects the cut is large.

blocks.md:
**Minimising a corpus** means finding a small subset with the same coverage. AFL does it continuously: it gives each queue entry a score from its execution time and file size, then for every tuple picks the best-scoring entry that covers it. These *favored* entries, usually 5 to 10 times fewer than the whole queue, get most of the fuzzing time; others are skipped 75 to 99 percent of the time. `afl-cmin` and libFuzzer's `-merge=1` do a one-off version that permanently discards redundant files.

The figure shows how a corpus grows over a real 60-second run of the FuzzedDataProvider harness on the *fixed* parser: fast at first, then a long plateau.

blocks.title: Corpus growth over 7.3 million executions (real run)

scenes.caption: Coverage (cov) at 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 executions: 36, 52, 53, 80 edges. Most of the parser is reached in the first 10,000 inputs.
After 100,000 executions coverage never moves again: 82 edges for the remaining 7.2 million runs. A plateau like this says 'improve the harness or seeds', not 'run longer'.
The corpus keeps growing (64, 113, 149, 152 inputs) through hit-count and size changes, not new edges. This is what minimisation later trims.

blocks.md: Seeds change results more than people expect. Klees et al. (lesson 9) found AFLFast produced over 1,000 crashing inputs on `nm` from an empty seed but only 24 from a small valid seed, statistically the same as AFL's 23. Always report which seeds you used.

A good campaign starts with small valid seeds per feature, a dictionary of the format's tokens, and a minimised corpus that you keep and reuse. When coverage plateaus, improve the inputs and harness rather than adding CPU time.

blocks.question: Coverage has not increased for six hours, but the corpus keeps gaining entries. What is the most useful next step?
options: Run for another week on the same setup
Read a coverage report, find unreached code, then add seeds, dictionary tokens or harness changes that target it
Delete the corpus and restart from empty
Turn off the sanitizer to run faster
blocks.explain: A plateau means the current mutations cannot reach new code. New corpus entries are hit-count and size variants. Targeted seeds, tokens or a harness change move the plateau; more time on the same setup rarely does.

blocks.question: What does libFuzzer's -merge=1 MIN corpus/ do?
options: Copies into MIN only the inputs from corpus/ that add coverage not already in MIN
Deletes crashing inputs from corpus/
Merges two fuzzers into one process
Minimises each input to its smallest size
blocks.explain: The docs: inputs from the second and later directories that trigger new coverage are merged into the first. It shrinks a corpus to a coverage-equivalent subset; per-input shrinking is a different feature (-minimize_crash or reduce_inputs).

lessons.title: Crash triage: deduplicate, minimise, root-cause, fix

blocks.md:
A day of fuzzing can leave thousands of crash files. Most describe the same few bugs. **Triage** turns the pile into a short list of distinct, understood bugs, in four steps:

1. **Deduplicate**: group crashes that are the same bug.
2. **Minimise**: shrink each representative input to the smallest one that still fails.
3. **Root-cause**: find the faulty line and the wrong assumption.
4. **Fix and test**: patch, then turn the reproducer into a regression test.

Deduplication is harder than it sounds. AFL's whitepaper notes that grouping by faulting address lumps unrelated bugs together when they all crash inside `strcpy`, while hashing the whole call stack inflates counts when one bug is reachable along many paths. A common compromise is a **stack hash**: hash the top few frames of the crashing stack, ignoring the fuzzer's own frames. ClusterFuzz advertises accurate crash deduplication along these lines.

**Minimisation** cuts an input down while the same crash still happens. libFuzzer's `-minimize_crash=1` keeps mutating and keeps only smaller inputs that still crash; AFL's `afl-tmin` zeroes and deletes blocks of decreasing size, then normalises bytes (it uses the ASCII digit '0' rather than a zero byte, to keep text formats parseable). The real run on this course's crash:

blocks.code:
$ ./fuzz_tlv -minimize_crash=1 -runs=20000 -exact_artifact_path=min.bin crash-fdaa623c...
CRASH_MIN: minimizing crash input: 'crash-fdaa623c1525f0600847bbdb20a0edb07a40f84b' (114 bytes)
...
CRASH_MIN: failed to minimize beyond min.bin (29 bytes), exiting

$ xxd min.bin
00000000: 544c 5631 4e17 0000 0001 0000 0000 0000  TLV1N...........
00000010: 214e 4e4e 4e4e 4e4e 4e4e 4e4e 4e         !NNNNNNNNNNNN

$ ./fuzz_tlv min.bin
==36105==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x603000001d64 ...
WRITE of size 23 at 0x603000001d64 thread T0
    #1 0x000100e68b78 in parse_tlv tlv.c:16
    #2 0x000100e68e00 in LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput fuzz_tlv.c:10
0x603000001d64 is located 0 bytes after 20-byte region [0x603000001d50,0x603000001d64)
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 0x000100e68dec in LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput fuzz_tlv.c:9
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow tlv.c:16 in parse_tlv
blocks.caption: Real output, trimmed. 114 bytes became 29: the magic, one N record with length hex 17 (23), and 23 value bytes. The leftover byte values are noise the minimiser had no reason to change.

blocks.md:
Now read the report like a detective, line by line:

- **What**: heap-buffer-overflow, a WRITE of 23 bytes.
- **Where**: `parse_tlv` at tlv.c line 16, the `memcpy` into `out->name`.
- **Which object**: the address is "0 bytes after" a **20-byte** region allocated in the harness at line 9. That is `struct rec`: 16 bytes of name plus a 4-byte count.
- **Input**: the length byte is 23.

So the root cause is a broken assumption: the code checks that `len` bytes exist in the *input*, never that they fit in the *destination*. A **debugger** (lldb on macOS, gdb on Linux) confirms this in the concept sense: run the reproducer, stop at a breakpoint on the `memcpy` line, print `len` and `sizeof out->name`, and watch the comparison that should have been there. The trace below steps through exactly that.

blocks.title: Root-causing parse_tlv with the 29-byte reproducer

scenes.caption: 29 bytes arrive. The first 4 are TLV1, so the magic check passes.
The cursor i starts after the magic. 4 + 2 <= 29, so the loop reads one record header.
The header says type 'N', length 23.
The value check: 6 + 23 = 29, not greater than 29. The value fits in the input, so the check passes. It is the only length check.
memcpy copies 23 bytes into name[16]: 4 bytes clobber count, 3 land past the 20-byte struct. ASan stops here: root cause found.
scenes.output:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 23 ... in parse_tlv tlv.c:16

blocks.caption: The fix compares the length with the destination, the assumption that was missing, and rejects rather than truncates so callers learn the record was bad. The test pins the reproducer and both sides of the boundary. All output is real.

blocks.md: Two more triage tools matter at scale. **Bisection** finds the commit that introduced a bug by testing the reproducer against builds in between a good and a bad version (ClusterFuzz does this automatically for regression ranges). And the reproducer itself should live on: commit it to the project's fuzzing corpus or test data so every future build runs it. Go does this for you, as lesson 11 shows.

Write the root cause as one sentence before writing the fix: "parse_tlv trusts the record length when copying into the 16-byte name field." If you cannot, you have found a symptom, not the cause, and the fix will likely miss variants.

blocks.question: Two crash files both end in memcpy inside parse_tlv, but one is reached from load_config() and one from load_profile(). How should a stack-hash deduplicator with the top 3 frames treat them?
options: Always as one bug, because the faulting line is the same
As zero bugs, because memcpy is a library function
As two separate buckets, since frame 3 (the caller of parse_tlv) differs, even though they may be one root cause
It cannot hash them without source code
blocks.explain: Stack hashes include callers, so different paths into the same bug make different buckets. That is the over-counting Klees et al. measured. A human or a fix-based check (does one patch fix both?) merges them.

blocks.question: Why does the fix return -1 for len > 16 instead of copying only the first 16 bytes?
options: Truncation is slower
memcpy cannot copy fewer bytes than requested
Returning -1 is required by ASan
Silently truncating hides malformed input from the caller and changes data without telling anyone; rejecting makes the error visible
blocks.explain: Both stop the overflow. Rejecting keeps the parser honest about invalid input. Truncation can be right for some formats, but it should be a deliberate decision, documented and tested.

lessons.title: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics

blocks.md:
Everyone wants to know which fuzzer, harness or setting is better. In 2018 George Klees, Andrew Ruef, Benji Cooper, Shiyi Wei and Michael Hicks, researchers at the University of Maryland and the University of Texas at Dallas, examined the experimental evaluations in 32 fuzzing papers in *Evaluating Fuzz Testing* (ACM CCS 2018). They found problems in every one, then ran their own large experiment with AFL and AFLFast (a variant that changes which corpus entries get fuzzed most) to show the problems change conclusions.

The tiny example first. Run the same fuzzer twice on the same program with the same seed and you get different results, because mutation is random. On `nm`, one AFL run found just over 1,200 crashing inputs and one AFLFast run about 800, so AFL looks better. The medians over 30 runs each told the opposite story: about 400 for AFL and close to 1,250 for AFLFast.

blocks.title: Crashes found in gif2png, empty seed (Klees et al. 2018)

scenes.caption: After 13 hours: AFL has found no crashes, AFLFast nearly 40 (drawn at 40). A 13-hour paper would declare AFLFast far better.
After 24 hours: AFL 39, AFLFast 52. The gap has nearly closed, and for nm with a non-empty seed the paper saw the lead reverse between 6 and 24 hours.
Even the 24-hour medians (AFLFast 51, AFL 39 over 30 runs) differed by too little for the Mann Whitney U test to call significant. Same numbers, no conclusion.

blocks.md:
The paper's recommendations, in order:

1. **Multiple trials and a statistical test.** They ran at least 30 trials per configuration and recommend the **Mann Whitney U test**, a non-parametric test (it does not assume the results follow a bell curve) for whether one fuzzer's results tend to be larger than another's.
2. **Long runs.** At least 24 hours; 11 of the 32 papers used runs under 5 or 6 hours.
3. **Several seeds**, stated precisely, including the empty seed.
4. **Ground truth for bugs, not "unique crashes".** They applied every later patch to `cxxfilt`: all 57,142 crashing inputs that AFL's coverage-profile heuristic called unique were fixed by just **9** distinct patches. Stack hashes did better (about 46 hashes where coverage said 500) but still over-counted, and about 16 percent of hashes for one bug were shared with another bug.
5. **A common, diverse benchmark** instead of a few hand-picked programs.

**Coverage over time** is the everyday measure you will use on your own campaigns. Plot covered edges against wall-clock time or executions; a curve that is still rising says keep going, a flat one says change something (lesson 7). Coverage is a proxy: the paper cites evidence that more coverage correlates with more bugs, but weakly, so bugs found against known ground truth are the stronger measure when you compare tools.
"Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.
To compare two fuzzing setups: 30 or more runs each, at least 24 hours, the same documented seeds, a statistical test, and bugs counted by distinct fixes. Anything less is an anecdote.

blocks.prompt: A teammate ran your new harness once for 2 hours and the old one once for 2 hours. The new one found 140 unique crashes, the old one 35. What can you conclude?
blocks.reveal: Very little. One run each cannot separate the harness from luck, 2 hours is short enough that rankings flip later, and 140 unique crashes may be a handful of bugs. Rerun both many times for longer, test the difference statistically, and triage the crashes into distinct bugs (ideally by which fix resolves each).

blocks.question: Why did Klees et al. recommend the Mann Whitney U test rather than comparing average crash counts?
options: Fuzzing results vary widely between runs and are not normally distributed, so a non-parametric test tells whether a difference is likely real
It runs faster than computing an average
It counts unique bugs automatically
Averages cannot be computed for crash counts
blocks.explain: Run-to-run variance is large and skewed. Averages can differ by chance; the test estimates whether one configuration's results tend to exceed the other's, without assuming a bell curve.

blocks.question: All 57,142 'unique' crashing inputs in cxxfilt were fixed by 9 patches. What does that measure?
options: That cxxfilt had 57,142 bugs
The speed of AFL
How badly coverage-profile deduplication over-counts real bugs
That stack hashing is perfect
blocks.explain: Grouping by fixing patch gives ground truth: 9 conceptual bugs. The heuristic inflated the count by thousands of times.

lessons.title: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed

blocks.md:
Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) is where modern continuous fuzzing begins. The memory-safety-bugs course covered the bug: OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat code copied as many bytes as a length field claimed, leaking server memory to anyone who asked. The bug entered OpenSSL in December 2011, shipped in 1.0.1 on 14 March 2012, and was fixed in 1.0.1g on 7 April 2014.

It was found independently by two parties. A team of security engineers at Codenomicon (Riku, Antti and Matti) found it while improving the SafeGuard feature of their Defensics protocol testing tools, and reported it through NCSC-FI (the National Cyber Security Centre of Finland) for coordination. Neel Mehta of Google Security found it too and was the first to report it to the OpenSSL team. Because of the coincident discovery, Codenomicon was also assigned a duplicate identifier, CVE-2014-0346, which should not be used.

The OSS-Fuzz documentation states it plainly: **OSS-Fuzz** (open-source software fuzzing) "was launched in 2016 in response to the Heartbleed vulnerability", a relatively simple bug that fuzzing could have found, at a time when fuzzing was cumbersome and rare. It is a free Google service that builds fuzz targets for open-source projects, runs them continuously, and privately reports bugs to the maintainers. The [ClusterFuzz documentation](https://google.github.io/clusterfuzz/setting-up-fuzzing/heartbleed-example/) even has a tutorial that rebuilds OpenSSL 1.0.1f with ASan and a libFuzzer handshake target to find Heartbleed.

The engine underneath is **ClusterFuzz**, a scalable fuzzing infrastructure that Google uses for all its products and as OSS-Fuzz's backend. Its documentation lists what it automates: running libFuzzer, AFL++ and Honggfuzz (another Google coverage-guided fuzzer) across a cluster (Google's instance runs on 30,000 VMs), deduplicating crashes, minimising testcases, bisecting regression ranges, and filing, triaging and closing bugs.

blocks.title: How a bug moves through OSS-Fuzz

scenes.caption: The project adds fuzz targets and a build script to OSS-Fuzz. OSS-Fuzz rebuilds the project from its latest source with sanitizers.
Bots fuzz around the clock with several engines, sharing a corpus. A crash is deduplicated, minimised and bisected to a commit range.
A private issue goes to the maintainer with the reproducer and stack trace. The 90-day disclosure clock starts.
The maintainer lands a fix. ClusterFuzz re-runs the testcase on new builds, sees it no longer crashes, and marks the issue verified.
The issue becomes public after the fix ships or at 90 days, whichever comes first (with a 14-day grace period if a fix is scheduled).

blocks.title: OSS-Fuzz trophy counts as published by the project

scenes.caption: OSS-Fuzz docs: as of August 2023, over 10,000 vulnerabilities and 36,000 bugs fixed across 1,000 projects.
The project README: as of May 2025, over 13,000 vulnerabilities and 50,000 bugs across 1,000 projects. These are the project's own counts of identified and fixed issues.

blocks.md:
**Cloudbleed (2017)**, a nickname echoing Heartbleed (Ormandy's report calls it "kinda like heartbleed"), shows that fuzzing infrastructure finds bugs in unexpected ways. On 17 February 2017 Tavis Ormandy of Google Project Zero (Google's vulnerability research team) was working on *corpus distillation*: collecting public web data to build fuzzing corpora. Some of the data made no sense: it contained chunks of uninitialised memory with cookies, keys and other users' requests from Cloudflare's reverse proxies. Ormandy reached Cloudflare urgently through Twitter.

Cloudflare's report gives the root cause: generated C code from Ragel (a state-machine compiler) checked for the end of the buffer with `==` instead of `>=`, and a parser bug let the pointer jump past the end. Cloudflare had an initial mitigation in 47 minutes and a global fix in under 7 hours. At peak, about 1 in every 3,300,000 requests could leak memory, and leaked pages had been cached by search engines. Afterwards part of Cloudflare's security team fuzzed the generated parser code to look for similar overruns.

blocks.caption: One character of difference. A >= check still catches a pointer that jumped over the end; an == check only catches one that lands exactly on it.

blocks.md: Continuous fuzzing turns fuzzing from an event into a property of the project: every commit is fuzzed, every crash is triaged, and fixed reproducers keep guarding the code. If your project parses untrusted input, it belongs in OSS-Fuzz or a ClusterFuzzLite setup in CI.

blocks.question: Why does ClusterFuzz bisect each crash to a commit range?
options: To decide the CVE number
To tell maintainers which change introduced the bug, which speeds up the fix and shows which releases are affected
To make the fuzzer run faster
Bisection removes duplicate crashes
blocks.explain: Knowing the introducing commit narrows the search for the root cause and answers the first question users ask: which versions are vulnerable?

blocks.question: How was Cloudbleed actually discovered?
options: A fuzzer crashed Cloudflare's edge servers
Cloudflare's monitoring alerted on high memory use
A customer reported a wrong page
Data gathered for fuzzing corpora contained leaked memory that did not match what Tavis Ormandy expected
blocks.explain: Ormandy's Project Zero report describes a corpus distillation project: public data collected to build fuzzing corpora contained uninitialised memory. Fuzzing infrastructure found it, but not by crashing anything.

lessons.title: Fuzzing beyond C: Go, Rust, Python and property-based testing

blocks.md:
Memory-safe languages do not overflow buffers silently, but they still crash, hang, throw unexpected exceptions and compute wrong answers. In those languages the fuzzer's oracle becomes a **panic** (Go and Rust's term for an unrecoverable run-time error), an **uncaught exception**, or a property that the code must always satisfy.

**Go** has had fuzzing in its standard toolchain since Go 1.18. A fuzz test is a function `FuzzXxx(f *testing.F)` in a `_test.go` file; `f.Add` supplies seeds and `f.Fuzz` the target. It is coverage-guided on amd64 and arm64. Here is the TLV parser ported to Go, with a different planted bug: the bounds check is missing entirely.

blocks.caption: Real run with Go 1.24 on the course Mac. 'TLV1000' means type '0' with length '0', which is byte 48, so the slice asks for bytes up to 54 of a 7-byte input.

blocks.md:
Go writes every failing input into `testdata/fuzz/<FuzzTest>/`, and a plain `go test` (no `-fuzz` flag) runs every file there as an ordinary test. Commit that directory and the crash is a **regression test** forever. On the real run, plain `go test` first failed on `FuzzParse/0de5af40ef3b102a` with the same panic; after adding `if i+n > len(b) { return r, errors.New("value runs past end") }` it passed, and a further 20-second fuzz run did 1.9 million executions without failure.

**Rust** uses [cargo-fuzz](https://rust-fuzz.github.io/book/cargo-fuzz.html), which the Rust Fuzz Book calls the recommended tool: it is not itself a fuzzer but invokes libFuzzer through the `libfuzzer-sys` crate. Targets live in a `fuzz/` directory and run with `cargo fuzz run <target>`; in Rust the typical findings are panics, integer overflow in debug builds, infinite loops and bugs in `unsafe` code.

**Python** has **Atheris**, Google's coverage-guided Python fuzzer based on libFuzzer. It instruments Python bytecode and can also fuzz native C extensions. The harness wraps imports in `atheris.instrument_imports()`, defines `TestOneInput(data)`, and catches only the exceptions the code documents; anything else is reported as a crash.

blocks.code:
# tlvlib.py
def decode(blob: bytes) -> str:
    if blob[:5] != b"TLV1N":
        raise ValueError("bad magic")
    n = blob[5]                    # BUG: IndexError if blob is exactly 5 bytes
    value = blob[6:6 + n]
    if len(value) != n:
        raise ValueError("truncated")
    return value.decode("utf-8", errors="strict")

# fuzz_tlv.py
import sys, atheris
with atheris.instrument_imports():
    import tlvlib

def TestOneInput(data: bytes):
    try:
        tlvlib.decode(data)
    except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        pass                       # documented, expected errors

atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput)
atheris.Fuzz()

$ python fuzz_tlv.py -seed=1 -artifact_prefix=py-
#566  NEW  cov: 4 ft: 4 corp: 2/7b ... MS: 4 CopyPart-ChangeByte-ShuffleBytes-CMP- DE: "TLV1N"-
 === Uncaught Python exception: ===
IndexError: index out of range
    n = blob[5]                          # BUG: IndexError if blob is exactly 5 bytes
Test unit written to py-crash-3a804638e24e773722b606da621cf5f6708cd5ed
Base64: VExWMU4=
blocks.caption: Real run (Atheris on Python 3.12, trimmed). The crash input is exactly the five bytes TLV1N. An earlier version written with blob.startswith(b"TLV1N") was still unsolved after two minutes; with the slice comparison the log shows the token learned (DE: "TLV1N").

blocks.md: **Property-based testing** is fuzzing's close cousin. Instead of hunting crashes, you state a *property* that must hold for every input, and a library generates inputs to break it. **Hypothesis**, "the property-based testing library for Python", generates values from *strategies* (`st.text()`, `st.lists(st.integers())` and so on) and, when a test fails, **shrinks** the failing example to a minimal one. A classic property is a round trip: decoding what you encoded gives back the original.

blocks.caption: Real output (Hypothesis 6.170, trimmed). Both failures shrink to the first character that needs two UTF-8 bytes, U+0080. The fix: write len(data), the byte count, and reject names over 255 bytes.

blocks.title: Hypothesis shrinking: why U+0080 is the minimal failure

scenes.caption: ASCII names work: 'ab' is 2 characters and 2 UTF-8 bytes, so the length byte 02 is right and decoding returns 'ab'.
U+0080 is 1 character but 2 UTF-8 bytes (c2 80). The length byte says 01, so decode reads only c2: invalid UTF-8.
Shrinking tried smaller code points and shorter strings; U+0080 is the smallest character that encodes to 2 bytes, so Hypothesis reports exactly that.
Fixed: the length byte is len(data) = 02, both bytes are read, and the round trip holds for every string up to 255 bytes.

blocks.md: Property tests and fuzz targets combine well. Hypothesis has a documented hook (`fuzz_one_input`) for driving a property test from an external fuzzer, and OSS-Fuzz accepts Go, Rust, Python, Java and JavaScript projects as well as C and C++.

blocks.question: In Go, what turns a fuzzer-found crash into a permanent regression test?
options: You must copy the input into a new unit test by hand
Go saves it under testdata/fuzz/<FuzzTest>/, and plain go test runs every file there
The crash is uploaded to OSS-Fuzz
go vet reruns old crashes
blocks.explain: The Go docs: by default go test runs every seed corpus entry, including files in testdata/fuzz, as a unit test. Commit the file with the fix and the bug cannot quietly return.

blocks.question: What is the oracle in the Hypothesis example?
options: The property decode(encode(name)) == name, which must hold for every generated string
A crash or hang
AddressSanitizer
Code coverage
blocks.explain: Property-based testing finds wrong answers, not just crashes. The round-trip property caught a bug that never crashes in Python's memory-safe runtime: the length byte counts characters instead of bytes.

lessons.title: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case

blocks.md:
Files are easy to fuzz: one input, one run. Network protocols are harder because they are **stateful**: what a server does with a message depends on what came before. An FTP (File Transfer Protocol) server only accepts a file listing after a successful login; a TLS server only processes application data after a handshake. A fuzzer that mutates single messages mostly produces garbage that the server rejects in its first state, and never reaches the code behind the login.

Stateful fuzzers therefore fuzz **sequences**. AFLNet, a research fuzzer by Van-Thuan Pham, Marcel Böhme and Abhik Roychoudhury (ICST 2020), shows the idea. Per its [README](https://github.com/aflnet/aflnet), it is seeded with recorded message exchanges between a real client and the server, replays mutated variations of the sequence, and uses the server's **response codes** as feedback about which state was reached, alongside code coverage. Sequences that reach new states or new code are kept, exactly like AFL keeps files.

blocks.title: Why stateful fuzzing mutates late messages (toy FTP-like server)

scenes.caption: A recorded session is the seed: login, then a listing. Each response code names the state the server reached.
Mutating the first message gets '500' every time: the server stays in its start state, so the code behind login is never fuzzed.
Instead, replay the valid prefix unchanged and mutate only the message after it. Now the fuzzed bytes reach the logged-in state's parser.
A new response code (or new coverage) marks a new state. That sequence joins the corpus and becomes the prefix for deeper fuzzing.

blocks.md:
Generation-based protocol tools take the other route: a model of the protocol's messages and states. Codenomicon's Defensics, which found Heartbleed, is a commercial example. Either way, the hard parts of protocol fuzzing are the same:

- **Speed**: each test needs network round trips and often a fresh server, so thousands per second is good where file fuzzers do hundreds of thousands.
- **State reset**: leftover state from one sequence (an open session, a cache) must not leak into the next, or results do not reproduce.
- **Oracles**: a crashed daemon is obvious, but a firmware chip that silently reboots may not be. Researchers often watch logs, heartbeats or a debug interface.

**Project Zero's Broadcom Wi-Fi research (2017)** shows where protocol bugs hide. Gal Beniamini, a Project Zero researcher, studied the firmware running *inside* Broadcom's Wi-Fi chips, a separate ARM processor that handles much of the Wi-Fi protocol itself so the phone's main processor does not have to. Beniamini extracted the firmware, used symbols from the open-source NexMon project and Broadcom's open-source SoftMAC driver to understand it, and the BinDiff binary comparison tool to carry symbol names across firmware versions.

Reviewing the code that handles *information elements* (the tagged fields inside Wi-Fi management frames) turned up several vulnerabilities, including simple stack overflows, and two heap overflows in TDLS (Tunneled Direct Link Setup, which lets two devices on one network talk directly), triggerable by any peer on the network with no user action. The firmware's operating system used no stack cookies. All were disclosed to Broadcom, which the post credits as very responsive; the demonstration used a then fully updated Nexus 6P.

The Broadcom case was found by reverse engineering and code review, not fuzzing, and its lesson for fuzzers is about reach: the dangerous code ran only for specific frame types in specific connection states. A stateless fuzzer of single frames would rarely get there.

Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

blocks.question: Why does AFLNet use the server's response codes as feedback, in addition to code coverage?
options: Response codes are faster to compute than coverage
They replace the need for seeds
They reveal which protocol state the server reached, so sequences reaching new states are kept even when coverage alone is ambiguous
They detect memory corruption
blocks.explain: Its README describes identifying server states from response codes and steering towards progressive regions of the state space. State feedback complements coverage: the same code can run in different states.

blocks.question: A fuzzer for a Wi-Fi chip mutates single management frames from a fresh, unassociated state and finds nothing in a week. What is the most likely gap?
options: The firmware has no bugs
Wi-Fi cannot be fuzzed
The sanitizer is missing
The vulnerable handlers run only in later states (associated, TDLS set up), which single frames from the start state never reach
blocks.explain: As in the Broadcom research, the interesting parsers sit behind protocol state. Replay a valid setup sequence, then mutate the frames that arrive afterwards.

lessons.title: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input

blocks.md:
Some checks are nearly impossible to pass by mutation. Consider a parser that reads a 32-bit number `x` from its input and only reaches the bug if `x * 7 + 3 == 0x1A2B3C4D`. Exactly one of the 4,294,967,296 possible values passes. Random mutation hits it about once per four billion tries; comparison tracing does not help much either, because the program compares `x * 7 + 3`, not `x`, with the constant.

**Symbolic execution** attacks this differently. Instead of running the program on a concrete number, it runs it on a *symbol* `x` that stands for every possible value. Each operation builds an expression (`x * 7 + 3`), and at each branch the engine records the condition needed to go each way. The conjunction of conditions along one path is its **path condition**. To get an input for a path, hand its path condition to a solver.

The solver is an **SMT** solver (Satisfiability Modulo Theories: deciding whether a logical formula can be made true, where the formula may use *theories* such as integer arithmetic, arrays or fixed-width bit vectors, not just true and false variables). **Z3**, a theorem prover from Microsoft Research, is the most widely used. Its default input language is SMT-LIB2, the standard format of the [SMT-LIB](https://smt-lib.org/) initiative. Machine integers are modelled as bit vectors, so arithmetic wraps exactly as it does in C.

blocks.code:
from z3 import BitVec, Solver, ULE, sat

# Path to the bug in C:  uint32_t x = read_u32(input);
#   if (x * 7 + 3 == 0x1A2B3C4D) { if (x < 0x80000000) bug(); }
x = BitVec("x", 32)            # 32-bit machine integer: arithmetic wraps mod 2^32
s = Solver()
s.add(x * 7 + 3 == 0x1A2B3C4D)
s.add(ULE(x, 0x7FFFFFFF))      # unsigned x <= 0x7FFFFFFF, i.e. x < 0x80000000
print(s.check())
if s.check() == sat:
    v = s.model()[x].as_long()
    print(hex(v), (v * 7 + 3) % 2**32 == 0x1A2B3C4D)

# real output (z3-solver 5.4 via pip):
# sat
# 0x4ce19ae6 True
blocks.caption: The solver returns sat (satisfiable) and a model: x = 0x4ce19ae6. Because 7 is odd it has an inverse modulo 2 to the 32, so this is the only solution, and it happens to be below 0x80000000.

blocks.title: Symbolic execution forks at each branch and solves each path

scenes.caption: The input is a symbol, not a value. Every value of x is still possible.
At the first branch the engine forks. Each side carries its own path condition: x*7+3 == C on one side, its negation on the other.
The true side forks again. Reaching bug() needs both conditions: x*7+3 == C and x < 0x80000000.
The solver turns each path condition into a concrete test input. For the bug path: x = 0x4ce19ae6. Running the real program on it reproduces the bug.

blocks.md:
**KLEE**, by Cristian Cadar, Daniel Dunbar and Dawson Engler at Stanford (OSDI 2008), made symbolic execution work on real programs. It runs on LLVM bitcode and models the environment (files, command-line arguments) symbolically. Its results on all 89 stand-alone programs in GNU Coreutils: generated tests averaged over 90 percent line coverage per tool (median over 94 percent), beating the developers' own hand-written test suites. Applied to 452 applications (over 430,000 lines), it found 56 serious bugs, including three in Coreutils that had been missed for over 15 years.

The paper also names the two classic problems. **Path explosion**: the number of paths grows exponentially with the number of branches, and loops make it unbounded. The **environment problem**: real code calls the operating system, the network and libraries whose behaviour must be modelled or executed concretely.

**Concolic execution** (concrete plus symbolic) is the practical compromise. Run the program on a real input, record the symbolic constraints along the path it actually took, then negate one branch condition and ask the solver for an input that goes the other way. Every new input is a real execution, so the environment problem shrinks. Microsoft Research's SAGE (Scalable Automated Guided Execution), which AFL's historical notes list among earlier solver-based work, worked this way.

Modern practice mixes the approaches: a coverage-guided fuzzer explores cheaply, and when it stalls at a hard comparison, a solver crafts the input that gets past it. libFuzzer's comparison tracing (lesson 4) is a lightweight cousin of the same idea.

Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

Symbolic execution turns 'find an input that reaches here' into a math problem: collect the path condition, give it to an SMT solver, get a concrete input. Concolic execution keeps one foot in real execution to stay practical.

blocks.question: A fuzzer stalls at the check `if (crc32(data) == header->crc)`. Why might symbolic execution also struggle here, while a FUZZING_BUILD_MODE build would not?
options: Solving for data that hashes to a given CRC through symbolic expressions of a whole loop is expensive, while the fuzzing build simply skips the check
Symbolic execution cannot handle any checksums
Fuzzing builds compute CRCs faster
SMT solvers do not support integers
blocks.explain: CRC32 is linear and solvable in principle, but expressed symbolically over a long buffer it is a heavy constraint. Disabling the check in a fuzzing-only build is far cheaper. For true cryptographic hashes, solving is infeasible.

blocks.question: What does a path condition contain?
options: The list of functions called on the path
The concrete input that reached the path
The conjunction of branch conditions that must hold for execution to follow that path
The coverage bitmap for the path
blocks.explain: Each branch adds its condition (or its negation). Any input satisfying all of them follows the path; the solver finds one such input.

lessons.title: Variant analysis and patch diffing: one bug, many siblings

blocks.md: A bug is rarely alone. The same programmer, the same API and the same wrong assumption usually appear in more than one place. **Variant analysis** is, in CodeQL's documentation's words, "the process of using a known security vulnerability as a seed to find similar problems in your code". The tiny example: the TLV project also has a profile parser, written by the same developer the same week.

blocks.caption: A sibling of the parse_tlv bug: same assumption, different field. Fixing parse_tlv alone would leave this one live.

blocks.md:
**CodeQL** is "a language and toolchain for code analysis" from GitHub. It first extracts the code into a database (a relational representation of every file), then runs queries written in QL, a declarative language that looks a little like SQL, against it. A variant query describes the *shape* of the bug, not one location. GitHub can then run a query across many repositories at once (*multi-repository variant analysis*).

The sketch below is modelled on the C/C++ query examples in the CodeQL docs (which find, for instance, `sprintf` called with a non-literal format string). It was not run for this course.

blocks.code:
/**
 * @name memcpy into a fixed-size field with a variable length
 * @kind problem
 * @id course/memcpy-fixed-field
 */
import cpp

from FunctionCall fc, FieldAccess dst
where fc.getTarget().getQualifiedName() = "memcpy"
  and dst = fc.getArgument(0)
  and dst.getTarget().getType().getUnspecifiedType() instanceof ArrayType
  and not fc.getArgument(2).isConstant()
select fc, "memcpy into fixed-size field " + dst.getTarget().getName() +
  " with a non-constant length: check it is bounded."
blocks.caption: Query sketch, not run here. As written it would flag both parse_tlv and parse_profile, and also the fixed parse_tlv: deciding whether a length is bounded needs CodeQL's range or guard analysis, so treat results as leads to triage, not verdicts.

blocks.title: Variant analysis: from one fixed bug to its siblings

nodes.label:
pattern:
length from input,
fixed-size dest

scenes.caption: Start from a bug you fully understand, with its root-cause sentence.
Abstract it: which source of data, which operation, which missing check. That is the pattern.
Encode the pattern as a query (or a grep, or a review checklist) and run it over the whole codebase.
Triage each result like a crash: parse_profile is a real sibling; the fixed parse_tlv is a false positive the query cannot yet tell apart.

blocks.md:
**Shellshock (2014)** is the textbook case for variants. Stephane Chazelas, a Unix specialist, discovered that Bash, when importing function definitions from environment variables, kept executing code that trailed the function body (CVE-2014-6271, disclosed on the oss-security mailing list by Florian Weimer on 24 September 2014). The first patch fixed that symptom. Within days Todd Sabin and Florian Weimer independently found a parser array overflow (CVE-2014-7186), Tavis Ormandy found another, and Michał Zalewski set up an AFL job seeded with a rudimentary function definition. Within hours AFL produced CVE-2014-6277 and, a few hours later, CVE-2014-6278, which gave straightforward command execution on systems protected only by the original patch.

The lasting fix was a design change, Florian Weimer's mitigation adopted in Bash 4.3 patch 27: exported functions get a recognisable name prefix, which, in Zalewski's words, shields the parser from untrusted inputs in normal use. The root cause was never one bug; it was *exposing a complex parser to untrusted environment variables*.

**Patch diffing** is variant analysis run backwards from someone else's fix. Compare the vulnerable and fixed versions and ask: what assumption did this patch add, and is it enforced everywhere it is needed? For open source this is a source diff; for closed software it is a binary diff with tools such as [BinDiff](https://github.com/google/bindiff), "an open-source comparison tool for binary files" that matches functions between two builds. Gal Beniamini's Broadcom research (lesson 12) used BinDiff to carry symbol names across firmware versions.

Defenders use patch diffing to check that a vendor's fix is complete, to find whether a vendored or forked copy of the code needs the same fix, and to write detection for the bug. The uncomfortable corollary: a public patch also tells attackers where the bug was, so the time between a patch's release and its installation is exposure.

When you fix a bug, write its pattern down and search for it before closing the ticket. Shellshock needed six CVEs because the first fix addressed one symptom of a design problem; variant analysis and fuzzing the patched code found the rest.

blocks.question: You fixed a missing length check in one message handler. What is the variant-analysis step?
options: Wait for a fuzzer to find other bugs
Describe the pattern (input length used without a destination bound) and search every handler for it, then triage the hits
Add a CVE number
Rewrite the fixed handler in another language
blocks.explain: Variant analysis uses the understood bug as a seed. The search can be a CodeQL query, a grep or a focused review; the point is to look for the same mistake everywhere.

blocks.question: Why did fuzzing find new Bash bugs after the first Shellshock patch?
options: The patch introduced them
AFL is better than code review at all bugs
The bugs were in a different program
The first patch only blocked one symptom; the function-import parser, still reachable from untrusted environment variables, had more bugs that AFL's coverage feedback explored
blocks.explain: Zalewski's write-up: AFL derived about 1,000 distinct test cases from one seed function definition and found CVE-2014-6277 and 6278 in the same parser. The robust fix stopped untrusted variables from reaching it.

lessons.title: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far

blocks.md:
Large language models (LLMs) now take part in vulnerability research on both sides. This lesson sticks to three documented cases and what each actually showed, because this area moves fast and claims outrun evidence.

**Case 1: Big Sleep and SQLite (2024).** Project Zero built a framework called Naptime for LLM-assisted vulnerability research; it evolved into **Big Sleep**, a collaboration between Project Zero and Google DeepMind. In late 2024 the team reported the agent's first real-world find: an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite. They reported it to the developers in early October, the developers fixed it the same day, and because the bug was not yet in an official release, no SQLite users were affected. The team said they believed it was the first public example of an AI agent finding a previously unknown exploitable memory-safety issue in widely used real-world software.

The method was variant analysis. The agent got a recent SQLite commit (message and diff) and was asked to review the current code for related issues that might not have been fixed. The bug it found: SQLite uses the sentinel value -1 in a field called `iColumn` to mean "the ROWID" (a table's internal row number). The `seriesBestIndex` function in the `generate_series` extension computed an index from that field without handling -1, then wrote into a 7-element stack array `aIdx` at a negative index. A debug `assert` caught it, but release builds compile assertions out. In the team's testing, the write landed below the array on the low 32 bits of a pointer that the next loop iteration used.

And recall lesson 5: OSS-Fuzz's harness did not enable `generate_series`, and 150 CPU-hours of AFL on the right binary still missed it. The team's own conclusion is measured: at present, a target-specific fuzzer would likely be at least as effective, but such an agent might uncover a distinct set of vulnerabilities.

blocks.title: The SQLite aIdx underflow, simplified (team's test build)

scenes.caption: aIdx[7] holds constraint numbers. In the team's build, the low half of the pConstraint pointer sat just below it. Layout varies by compiler and flags.
A normal constraint on column 1 gives iCol = 1, and aIdx[1] is written: in bounds.
A constraint on ROWID carries the sentinel -1, so iCol is negative. The debug assert(iCol>=0) would stop here; release builds have no assert.
aIdx[iCol] = i writes below the array, over the pointer's low bits. The next loop iteration dereferences the corrupted pointer: memory corruption.
The fix pattern: handle the -1 sentinel before using the value as an index. SQLite's developers fixed it the same day it was reported, before any release shipped it.

blocks.md:
**Case 2: AI-written fuzz harnesses in OSS-Fuzz (2023 to 2024).** Lesson 5 showed that a fuzzer only covers what its harness reaches, and writing harnesses is slow human work. In August 2023 the OSS-Fuzz team announced AI-powered fuzzing: prompt an LLM to draft a fuzz target for an uncovered function and feed compilation errors back until it builds. The pipeline later added running each new target briefly to weed out targets that crash instantly (a bug in the target, not the project) and help with triage. By November 2024 the pipeline had gained coverage in 272 C/C++ projects (up from 160), added over 370,000 lines of new coverage and found 26 new vulnerabilities, including CVE-2024-9143 in OpenSSL. The team says that bug had likely been present for two decades and would not have been found by the existing human-written targets.

Note what the AI did here: it wrote harnesses. The bugs were still found by fuzzing with sanitizers, and every report came with a reproducer.

**Case 3: an AI-built zero-day in the wild (2026).** A **zero-day** is a vulnerability that attackers exploit before the vendor has a fix. In May 2026 GTIG (Google Threat Intelligence Group) reported that, for the first time, it had identified a threat actor using a zero-day exploit it believed was developed with AI: a Python script that bypassed two-factor authentication (2FA) on a popular open-source, web-based system administration tool, given valid credentials. GTIG said the flaw was not memory corruption but a semantic logic error, a hardcoded trust assumption. Its evidence for AI authorship included abundant educational docstrings and a hallucinated CVSS score. GTIG worked with the vendor to disclose the bug and disrupt the planned mass exploitation, and stated that fuzzers and static analysis, built to find crashes and dangerous sinks, are not tuned for this kind of flaw.

LLMs produce confident, plausible text, including wrong code paths, invented functions and fake scores (the attacker's script above even hallucinated a CVSS rating). Never report an AI-suggested bug you have not reproduced yourself with a real input against a real build. The reproducer is the evidence; the explanation is commentary.

Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

blocks.question: In the OSS-Fuzz AI project, what did the language model contribute, and what found the bugs?
options: The model found and verified the bugs directly
The model wrote and repaired fuzz targets; coverage-guided fuzzing with sanitizers found the bugs and produced reproducers
The model replaced the sanitizers
The model chose which projects join OSS-Fuzz
blocks.explain: The pipeline generates targets, fixes compile errors, discards instantly crashing targets and then fuzzes. The vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2024-9143, came out of normal fuzzing of the new targets.

blocks.question: Why did OSS-Fuzz's long-running SQLite fuzzing miss the bug Big Sleep found?
options: The OSS-Fuzz harness was not built with the generate_series extension, and AFL on the right binary did not find it in 150 CPU-hours
SQLite has no fuzz targets
The bug only occurs on Windows
Fuzzers cannot find stack bugs
blocks.explain: The Big Sleep post: the harness configuration left the extension out, and a dedicated AFL attempt with the needed keywords still failed. Reach and difficulty, not lack of fuzzing, explain the miss.

lessons.title: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure

blocks.md:
A bug that the maintainers cannot reproduce does not get fixed. The OWASP vulnerability disclosure cheat sheet lists what an initial report should contain: enough detail to understand and reproduce the issue, supporting evidence, a proof of concept if available (for memory bugs, the minimised input and sanitizer output), the impact, and references. Write in clear, simple terms, since the reader may be a developer without a security background, and redact personal data from any evidence.

Here is a report for this course's bug, built from the real artefacts of lessons 4 and 8. The version numbers, commit and dates are illustrative.

blocks.code:
Title: Heap buffer overflow in parse_tlv() via oversized N record (tlv 1.2.0)

Summary
  parse_tlv() copies an N record's value into the 16-byte rec.name field
  using the record's length byte (0-255) without checking it against the
  field size. A crafted input writes up to 239 bytes past the field.

Affected
  tlv 1.0.0 to 1.2.0 (introduced in commit 3f2a9c1, found by bisection).

Reproduce
  clang -g -fsanitize=address tlv.c repro_main.c -o repro
  ./repro min.bin                        # 29-byte file attached
  ASan: heap-buffer-overflow, WRITE of size 23, parse_tlv tlv.c:16

Root cause
  Line 14 checks that len bytes exist in the input, never that they fit
  in out->name (16 bytes).

Impact
  Memory corruption of adjacent heap data in any program that parses
  untrusted TLV files. Exploitability not assessed.

Suggested fix (patch attached)
  Reject records with len > sizeof out->name; regression test attached.

Disclosure
  Reported privately on 2026-11-13. I plan to publish details 90 days
  after this report or when a fixed release ships, whichever is first,
  and am happy to coordinate a different date.
blocks.caption: A good report is short, reproducible and modest: it states what was shown (a write past the buffer) and does not claim more than that (exploitability was not assessed).

blocks.md:
**Where to send it.** Look for the project's security policy, a security advisory form, or a `security.txt` file. RFC 9116 (Request for Comments 9116, April 2022) defines `security.txt`: a text file at `/.well-known/security.txt` whose required `Contact` field says how to report vulnerabilities and whose required `Expires` field marks when the information goes stale. For open-source code, use the project's private reporting channel, never a public issue.

**Identifiers and severity.** A **CVE** (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) ID such as CVE-2014-0160 is the shared name for one vulnerability. IDs are assigned by **CNAs** (CVE Numbering Authorities), organisations authorised by the CVE Program, which the MITRE Corporation (a US non-profit) has run. Heartbleed shows why one shared name matters: Codenomicon's duplicate ID for the same bug had to be retired. **CVSS** (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), maintained by FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), rates severity from 0 to 10 from four metric groups: Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental.

**Timelines.** Coordinated disclosure needs a deadline, or fixes wait forever. Project Zero's current policy is "Full 90": the vendor has 90 days after notification to ship a patch, and details are published on day 90 *regardless of when the patch shipped*. Its examples: patch on day 47, details on day 90; no patch, details on day 90. If a bug is being exploited in the wild, details come out after 7 days. The policy page announces a move to 60 days on 2 February 2027 and 30 days on 3 January 2028, and records that exceptions were granted five times in 12 years. OSS-Fuzz opens reports after 90 days or when the fix is released, whichever is earlier, with a 14-day grace period if a fix is scheduled.

An **embargo** is an agreed period during which a fix is shared privately with those who must ship it before the public announcement. The Openwall `distros` lists, through which Linux and other operating system distributions coordinate, accept a maximum embargo of 14 days and prefer under 7.

blocks.title: Coordinated disclosure under a 90-day policy (Project Zero example)

scenes.caption: Day 0: a private report with reproducer, root cause and suggested fix. The 90-day clock starts.
The vendor triages, reserves a CVE through a CNA, develops and tests the fix. The researcher answers questions and checks the patch.
Days 40 to 47: distributions get the fix under embargo, within the distros list's 14-day maximum, so packages are ready on release day.
Day 47: patch and advisory with the CVE ID ship. Users can update. Under Full 90 the technical details still wait.
Day 90: the full write-up is published, giving users about six weeks to patch first. Had attackers exploited it in the wild, details would come at day 7.

blocks.md: **The defender's side.** If you maintain software, make reporting easy and safe: publish a `security.txt` or security policy with a monitored contact, state your scope and safe-harbour terms if you run a bounty, acknowledge reports quickly, and keep the reporter informed. When the fix ships, credit the reporter, publish an advisory with affected and fixed versions, and add the reproducer to your tests and fuzzing corpus. OWASP's cheat sheet also covers when a researcher gives up on an unresponsive vendor: options range from publishing anyway to reporting to a regulator to simply moving on.

Publishing a working exploit is a separate, debated decision (OWASP notes both sides). It is never needed to get a memory-safety bug fixed: the sanitizer report and minimised input are proof. This course's path ends at the fix and the advisory.

Report privately with a minimised reproducer, the sanitizer output, a one-sentence root cause and a suggested fix; agree a disclosure date; publish an advisory with versions and credit once users can patch.

**Practice legally, on code you control:**

- Google's [libFuzzer tutorial](https://github.com/google/fuzzing/blob/master/tutorial/libFuzzerTutorial.md) walks through harnesses, dictionaries and a Heartbleed exercise.
- [Fuzzing101](https://github.com/antonio-morales/Fuzzing101), a GitHub Security Lab initiative by Antonio Morales, is ten exercises that rediscover real CVEs in old versions of real software, mostly with AFL++.
- [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/) from Arizona State University covers program analysis and memory errors in a legal lab environment.
- When you are ready, integrate a project you contribute to with [OSS-Fuzz](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/getting-started/new-project-guide/) and keep its fuzzers healthy.

blocks.question: Under Project Zero's Full 90 policy, a vendor ships a patch on day 47. When are the technical details published?
options: Day 47, with the patch
Day 77, 30 days after the patch
Day 90
Never, once a patch exists
blocks.explain: Full X means details are published on day X regardless of when the patch shipped, unless the vendor asks for earlier release. Day 47 to day 90 is the window for users to update.

blocks.question: Which item does NOT belong in a first private report of a memory-safety bug?
options: The minimised reproducer and sanitizer output
The affected versions and a root-cause sentence
A suggested fix or pointer to guidance
A demand for payment before you share details
blocks.explain: OWASP warns that demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. Rewards belong in an established bug bounty programme with published terms.
